clue.text: Not the way you should enter this controversial broadcaster after a cold

definitions.text: Not the way you should enter this
definitions.note: a description of the answer's sense, pointing at this clue's own direction in the grid

indicators.note: after places the broadcaster's name behind the words that follow it in the clue

parts.note: taken as written
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
Jonathan Ross, the BBC presenter at the centre of several rows

explanation.surface: A warning to avoid a notorious TV presenter when you have a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a down clue, so the way not to enter it is sideways. The pieces read in order, the cold piece coming 'after' the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Since the entry runs vertically in the grid, writing it horizontally would be the wrong direction.

clue.text: Stimulating nice feel outside the church is what keeps a broadcaster going

indicators.note: outside tells us the mixed letters go round the next piece rather than beside it
stimulating means stirring up, so the following letters get stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A churchgoer's nice glow somehow keeps a broadcaster on air.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC is funded by a compulsory annual payment from every British household with a television.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC's money comes from the annual charge viewers pay to watch television, so that charge sustains it.

clue.text: Old rogue Blair as depicted in the Eye, losing head, in the shit, finished by Brown, ultimately

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: a childish word for excrement

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the last letter of Brown, as in Gordon

indicators.note: losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.words: Blair as depicted in the Eye
parts.note: Private Eye long portrayed Tony Blair as the trendy vicar of St Albion's parish

explanation.surface: A dig at Blair, satirised as a vicar, now humiliated and finished off by his successor Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's 'St Albion Parish News' cast Blair as the vicar; beheaded, he sits in the POO, and Brown's last letter ends it.
explanation.definitionFit: A picaroon is an archaic word for a scoundrel, pirate or adventurer living by his wits.

clue.text: What's vice to Bill? The bloody obvious failure to be self-serving

parts.note: Al Gore was vice-president to Bill Clinton
a truism is a statement too obvious to need saying

explanation.surface: A sneer at Clinton's vice and the obvious fact that politicians serve themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vice' looks like a sin, given Clinton's reputation, but here it is the office of vice-president.
explanation.definitionFit: Altruism is selfless concern for others, the opposite of acting in one's own interest.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) Lest, um, juggling with tits is a critical indication

indicators.note: juggling things tosses them about, so the letters land in a new order

parts.note: the letters of lest, um and tits, the juggling words aside

explanation.surface: A hesitant warning that a juggling act with breasts reveals a lot about someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is split around the indicator: lest and um before it, tits after.
explanation.definitionFit: A litmus test is a decisive check that reveals the true nature of something, from the chemistry acidity paper.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Indifferent Boris finally informed about one

indicators.note: finally picks out only the closing letter of the name before it

parts.note: the last letter of Boris

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word wraps around the next piece

parts.note: to be told is to be informed
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, at last told about someone, shows no interest.
explanation.definitionFit: Stolid describes someone impassive and unemotional, showing little reaction or concern.

clue.text: see 21dn.
Embraced by pain in the neck, subjected to a shagging — most ugly

indicators.note: something embraced is held inside arms, so this piece sits within the other

parts.note: a pest is an annoying person, a pain in the neck
having lain with someone, in the bedroom sense

explanation.surface: A crude remark about an unattractive person bedded by an annoying one.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain, said of a person's looks, is a polite word for unattractive, so the superlative fits.

clue.text: see 19dn.
Agree poor exploited taxpayer has to subsidise his entertainment?

definitions.text: taxpayer has to subsidise his entertainment?
definitions.note: a cryptic description: he is the one whose entertainment the taxpayer funds

indicators.note: exploited means used and worked over, so the letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that ordinary taxpayers fund the arts enjoyed by the well-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor exploited taxpayer' reads as one grievance, but poor is fodder and exploited the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera houses receive large public arts grants, so their patrons enjoy shows partly paid for by the public purse.

clue.text: Lords chief after spot that's a possible illicit sex venue

parts.note: the opening letter of Lords

explanation.definitionFit: Roadside lodgings that rent rooms anonymously are a cliché setting for secret affairs.

clue.text: Relief from oral sex exponent audibly expressed?

parts.note: one who sucks, said out loud

explanation.surface: A smutty line about getting relief from a practitioner of oral sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Succour means help or assistance given in time of hardship or distress.

clue.text: Unsavoury Cyclops on date after hot drink

indicators.note: on means placed next to, so the setter's letter is attached directly to the date
after sends the setter-and-date pair behind the words that follow it

parts.note: in fashion, the sense of 'hot right now'
a sip is a small drink
the setter refers to himself, so Cyclops is I
D is the abbreviation for date

explanation.surface: The setter, out on a date after a hot drink, is thoroughly unappetising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot drink' looks like tea, but the two words work separately. The setter's own name stands for the first person, I.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid food lacks flavour, so it has no savour; unsavoury here is taken literally.

clue.text: Corrupt Rolf "wrongly" in goal, primarily accommodated by Crown

indicators.note: being accommodated means being housed inside, so the pieces go into the next word

parts.note: the crown of the head is the pate

indicators.note: done wrongly means put in the wrong order, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: primarily means taking the first letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: the first letters of in and goal

explanation.surface: Rolf Harris, jailed by the Crown, wrongly sent down: a dig at his protestations.
explanation.walkthrough: Rolf Harris was convicted in 2014 and imprisoned; 'Crown' suggests the prosecution but is simply the top of the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Profligate means dissolute and recklessly extravagant, close to depraved or corrupt in conduct.

clue.text: see 19ac.
Instrument of ejaculation m-made contact with Brenda

parts.note: an ejaculation in the old sense is an exclamation
the stammered letter taken as written
to meet someone is to make contact
Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda; ER is Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A stammering account of someone overcome with excitement on meeting the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ejaculation' has its smutty sense in the surface but means only a cry here. Private Eye's nickname for Elizabeth II was Brenda.
explanation.definitionFit: This device measures electrical resistance in ohms, a piece of laboratory equipment.

clue.text: Unite, Boris nuts! No deserting the ill-suited leader

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild into a new order
deserting means abandoning, so those letters leave the group

parts.note: taken as written
these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A plea for unity in Johnson's camp, with nobody walking out on an unfit leader.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiberius, the reclusive and debauched second Roman emperor, is remembered as unfit to rule.

clue.text: (& 16ac.) Release on rejected Foreign Office lined up to be diluted by Cameron & co.?

definitions.text: to be diluted by Cameron & co.?
definitions.note: a cryptic description of the law the government wanted to weaken

parts.note: release from captivity is liberty

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the abbreviation is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: the usual abbreviation for the Foreign Office
things lined up are in formation

explanation.surface: A release about the Foreign Office being turned down and weakened by the Cameron government.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2015 Cameron's government set up a commission widely seen as an attempt to water down the Freedom of Information Act.
explanation.definitionFit: The Act gives the public a right to official records, which ministers sought to restrict.

clue.text: (& 10/24) Instinctively go off Labour's right wing (so few?), loony left having infiltrated

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so all the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: the right-hand half of the word Labour
taken as written
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Labour's dwindling right wing, infiltrated by the loony left, should trust its instincts and leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loony left' reads as a stock phrase, but loony is fodder and left gives just L; all four pieces are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow your nose is an idiom for acting on instinct or heading straight on without a plan.

clue.text: Lifeless organ, shrivelled all over

indicators.note: something all over another covers it on every side, so it wraps around it

parts.note: shrivelled and dried up
the ear is an organ of hearing

explanation.surface: A dead, withered organ, perhaps one past its prime.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary means dull and lacking liveliness or spirit, so dismal and flat.

clue.text: Not the main narrative of political party intervening in bust enhancement

indicators.note: intervening in means coming between, so one piece is placed inside the other

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust enhancement' reads as cosmetic surgery, but bust is the word to rearrange and enhancement the signal.

clue.text: (& 8ac.) God-backed catastrophe which led to downfall of Tory leader

definitions.text: which led to downfall of Tory leader
definitions.note: a relative clause describing the event rather than a noun

indicators.note: backed means put in reverse, so the god's name is read backwards

parts.note: the king of the Greek gods
a crisis is a disastrous turning point

explanation.surface: A divinely backed disaster that brought a Conservative prime minister down.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1956 Anthony Eden's failed invasion to seize the canal forced his resignation as prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1956 canal fiasco ruined Eden's premiership and led to his resignation the following year.

clue.text: Glossy crap with Yvette's end splitting political factions

parts.note: tat is cheap rubbish

indicators.note: splitting a pair means coming between them, so one letter sits inside

parts.note: left and right, abbreviated

indicators.note: the end of the name means its final letter only

explanation.walkthrough: A glossy is a slick magazine; Tatler is the British society magazine.

clue.text: Poor Nigel, independence lost for socially acceptable thrust

indicators.note: poor means in bad shape, so the name's letters are knocked out of order
lost for means given up in exchange, so one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: taken as written
I is the abbreviation for independent
U means upper-class, so acceptable in polite society

explanation.surface: Nigel Farage, his independence party fading, makes a push for respectability.
explanation.walkthrough: Nigel suggests Farage of the UK Independence Party. U for upper-class is an old British label for socially acceptable usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunge is a sudden forward movement, as with a sword or a body, the same as a thrust.

clue.text: see 19dn.
We're just producing an ejaculation on the parade ground

definitions.text: We're just producing an ejaculation on the parade ground

parts.note: surface reading: a crude confession of someone in the act
setter's reading: we are several first persons, plural of the letter, and just means correct
setter's reading: an ejaculation is a shouted exclamation, here a drill command

explanation.walkthrough: 'We' sounds like a crowd of first-person pronouns and 'just' means correct; together they say the command a sergeant barks.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the drill order telling marching soldiers to turn their heads to salute on the right.

clue.text: Stink about tennis player's rag?

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: BO is body odour
the player who serves in tennis

explanation.surface: A smelly tennis player's grubby towel.

explanation.definitionFit: Rag is a dismissive word for a newspaper, and the Observer is a long-running British Sunday title.

clue.text: Which will make your bum look big and tits depleted in the middle

the middle tells us where the removed letters sit, in the centre of the word

explanation.surface: Fashion advice about a garment that enlarges the backside while flattening the chest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the middle' tells us the two letters come from the centre of the longer word.
explanation.definitionFit: A bustle was a Victorian pad or frame worn under a skirt to puff out the back of the dress.
